title: Feathers in the wind
hook: a folk tale: gossip is like feathers from a pillow, impossible to gather back

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: motzi shem ra, bringing out a bad name. Your line was no false names. Did one false story get set straight? Today, a tale about how far words go once they leave. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-three.

A pillow, a knife, and a windy hill. That's the whole set for a story Jewish teachers tell about speech. Someone in a small town has been spreading talk about a neighbor. The talk turns out to be cruel, and the person feels sick about it and goes to the rabbi to ask how to make it right. The rabbi says: take a feather pillow up the hill, cut it open, and come back. Strange, but easy. The person climbs up, slits the pillow, watches the wind take the feathers, and comes back, ready to be forgiven. Good, says the rabbi. Now go and gather every feather.
screen: `A PILLOW, A KNIFE, A WINDY HILL.` → `CUT IT OPEN.` → `NOW GATHER EVERY FEATHER.`

segments.voice: Feathers in the wind. Turn the tale four ways. First, where it comes from. You won't find it in the Torah or the Talmud. It's a folk tale, and tellers hang it on different rabbis and different towns. That's worth saying plainly, because the tale doesn't need a famous source to land. It works because anyone who has ever opened a pillow knows how feathers behave. Second, the shape of the lesson. Scattering takes a moment. Gathering takes forever, and still fails. Words work the same way: they leave in a breath, then land in places you'll never see, in ears you'll never meet, and they get repeated in voices that aren't yours. Third, notice who the story is about. Not a villain. Someone who is sorry and wants to fix it. The tale doesn't say repentance is useless. Yesterday's lesson was about going back to set a story straight, and that matters. But the rabbi's point is that even real regret can't recall every feather. Some of the harm is already past reaching. Fourth, so the care belongs before the words. The book of Proverbs puts the stakes bluntly: "Death and life are in the power of the tongue." The tale turns that line into something you can see. And today a pillow opens with one tap. A forwarded message, a screenshot, a post: each one is a feather with a timestamp, blowing over hills the sender will never climb. The moment of most control is the second before speaking, while every feather is still inside.
screen: `A FOLK TALE, NOT A TALMUD PAGE.` · `EASY TO SCATTER, HARD TO GATHER.` · `EVEN REAL REGRET CAN'T RECALL THEM.` · `DEATH AND LIFE IN THE TONGUE.` · then, large: `YOU CAN'T GATHER FEATHERS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think before one sentence. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a conversation coming up today: a call, a meeting, a group chat, dinner. Is there one sentence you can already feel waiting on your tongue? A joke at someone's expense, a complaint about someone who won't be there, a piece of news that isn't yours to share. Hold that sentence like a pillow in your hands. Ask: once this is out, where could it blow? Then decide, now, while it's still sealed, whether it goes out at all. If you pray, you can ask in your own words for a guarded mouth. The bell holds the time.
Feathers in the wind. A folk tale: harmful words, like a pillow's feathers, scatter in a moment and can never all be gathered back. Today's word.
Your line: you can't gather feathers. Today, before one sentence about someone who isn't there, pause long enough to ask where it might blow. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Jewish teachers, parents and schools often tell the feathers tale when teaching about lashon hara, as a picture of why harmful speech can't be fully undone.
